# @qlairoslabs/acp-client

An embeddable, model-agnostic **Agent Client Protocol (ACP)** client: talk to AI coding
agents (Codex, Claude, Kimi, Pi, Gemini, Copilot, OpenCode, …) over JSON-RPC 2.0, with a
**degraded PTY fallback** for agents that don't speak ACP.

```ts
import { AgentController, ADAPTERS } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const agent = new AgentController({ adapter: ADAPTERS.codex, adapterId: "codex" });
await agent.start();
const { text } = await agent.prompt("Say hello in one sentence.");
console.log(text);
await agent.stop();
```

> **Runtime:** this package currently requires **[Bun](https://bun.sh) ≥ 1.3.5**.
> The transport layer is built on `Bun.spawn`. Node support is planned (see
> [Roadmap](#roadmap)); the spawn layer is already isolated behind a single module to make
> that a drop-in addition.

---

## Why this exists

ACP is a clean, model-agnostic way to drive coding agents, but the existing clients make
assumptions that don't fit when you orchestrate **many** agents across **many**
environments:

- **No forced `cwd` discovery.** Other libraries crawl up to the git root and impose a
  working directory. This one keeps target-visible `cwd` separate from an optional
  runtime `launcher` that prepares the exact host process.
- **Introspection over hardcoding.** Models, auth methods, capabilities, and config
  options are all *discovered* from the protocol at runtime, never baked in. The library
  surfaces raw protocol facts and lets you decide what they mean.
- **A fallback for agents that don't fully support ACP.** Some providers lack crucial
  operations (e.g. `login`), and some only expose ACP through an SDK that breaks
  subscription-based auth. For those, a **degraded mode** drives the agent's native
  interactive CLI through a PTY and parses the terminal output. It's expected to work worse
  than real ACP (hence "degraded") but it keeps the same output contract so your
  rendering code doesn't change.

---

## Install

```bash
# as a dependency in a Bun project
bun add @qlairoslabs/acp-client

# or for the CLI, globally
bun add -g @qlairoslabs/acp-client
```

---

## Core concepts

| Abstraction | What it is |
|---|---|
| **`AgentController`** | The control plane for **one** agent process: start/stop, prompt, interrupt, switch sessions, swap mode (normal ⇄ degraded), introspect capabilities & config. |
| **`AgentSession`** | A **durable conversation** with a stable identity that survives reconnects and mode-swaps. Wraps an `AgentController` and (optionally) records itself to a catalog. The front face for consumers that want persistence. |
| **`SessionManager` + `SessionStore`** | The session **catalog**: routing metadata (which adapter/mode/cwd a session belongs to), *not* conversation content. Merges your catalog with the agent's live `session/list`. Ships a `FileSessionStore`; inject your own (e.g. a database) for custom backends. |
| **Adapter** | Just how to *launch* an agent: the spawn command. `ADAPTERS` has convenience presets (`codex`, `claude`, `kimi`, `pi`, `gemini`, `copilot`, `opencode`); you can also pass a raw `{ command: [...] }`. Capabilities and commands are discovered after ACP initialization. |
| **Mode** | `"normal"` (real ACP over JSON-RPC) or `"degraded"` (drive the native CLI through a PTY and parse it). Both implement the same `AgentClient` output contract. |

---

## Usage

For an orchestration-oriented walkthrough covering catalog ownership, reopening logical
sessions, lifecycle listeners, handoff, harness commands, and reusable command routing,
see the [consumer guide](./CONSUMER_GUIDE.md).

### One-shot prompt

```ts
import {
  AgentController,
  ADAPTERS,
  createConsoleLogger,
  formatResponseMessages,
} from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const agent = new AgentController({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.codex,
  adapterId: "codex",
  cwd: process.cwd(),
  defaultPermission: "cancel",          // "approve" to auto-accept tool permissions
  logger: createConsoleLogger({ minLevel: "info" }),
});

const { sessionId, resumed } = await agent.start();
console.log(resumed ? "resumed" : "new", sessionId);

const result = await agent.prompt("Refactor utils.ts for readability.");
for (const message of result.messages) console.log(message.text);
console.log(result.stopReason, result.usage);

// If this application specifically needs a single string:
const displayText = formatResponseMessages(result.messages, "\n\n");

await agent.stop();
```

### Streaming activity (thinking / tool calls)

```ts
await agent.prompt("Find and fix the failing test.", {
  onChunk: (text) => process.stdout.write(text),         // response text as it streams
  onActivity: (event) => render(event),                  // thinking / tool calls / plan / …
  onUpdate: (raw) => log(raw),                           // every raw session/update, unmapped
  onPermissionRequest: (req) => {                        // blocking — the agent waits
    const allow = req.options.find((o) => o.kind === "allow_once");
    return allow ? { outcome: "selected", optionId: allow.optionId } : { outcome: "cancelled" };
  },
});
```

Always pick a permission option by **`kind`**, never by position or name. Option ids are
the agent's own strings, the order is the agent's choice — Claude lists its reject option
first — and `name` is prose meant for a human. The four kinds are `allow_once`,
`allow_always`, `reject_once`, `reject_always`; treat the `_always` pair as policy, since
they persist into the agent's settings and outlive the session.

If you omit `onPermissionRequest`, the client falls back to the controller's
`defaultPermission` (`"approve"` / `"cancel"`). `"approve"` selects `allow_once`, or
`allow_always` if that is the only grant offered, and cancels if it finds neither — it
never guesses.

Every session update except the response text reaches `onActivity`, discriminated by
`kind`: `thinking`, `user_message`, `tool`, `tool_update`, `plan`, `plan_update`,
`plan_removed`, `commands`, `mode`, `usage`, `session_info`, `config`, and `unknown` for
anything the protocol adds later (the raw payload rides along on `raw`).

**Tool calls arrive incrementally.** Agents announce a call before they know much about it
and fill it in afterwards, so the command, the diff and the output usually land on a later
`tool_update` — not on the initial `tool`. `event.content` is where the output lives —
`{type:"content"}` (with `text` pre-extracted for text blocks), `{type:"diff"}`,
`{type:"terminal"}`, or `{type:"other"}` with the raw payload for shapes we don't model.

You don't have to merge that yourself. `onRecord` hands you **full state** on every event:

```ts
await session.prompt("Find and fix the failing test.", {
  onRecord: ({ current, emitted }) => {
    if (current) render(current.recordId, current.event);  // always complete, never a delta
    // `emitted` is the subset worth keeping: announced → input → settled
  },
});
```

`onRecord` is `AgentSession`-only, because the session runs exactly **one** aggregator for
its lifetime and that is what makes `recordId`s stable. Holding a raw `AcpClient`? Build one
aggregator per stream and feed it from `onActivity`:

```ts
import { ActivityAggregator } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client/activity";

const agg = new ActivityAggregator();
onActivity: (event) => render(agg.apply(event));
```

If you do merge deltas by hand, two rules matter: absent fields mean *unchanged* (so
spreading is right), and `content`/`locations` **replace** the previous collection wholesale
— the schema says "replace the content collection", and agents that stream a growing tool
input resend the whole value each time.

### Sending activity over a wire

For a hub forwarding activity to a browser, send `wireFrames(result)` and fold with
`foldFrame`. Thinking crosses as a full record on the chunk that OPENS a block and as an
incremental `delta` for every chunk after it (re-sending the accumulated block per chunk is
quadratic — ~4 KB of text becomes ~800 KB over 400 chunks); everything else crosses as a
full record.

```ts
// hub
import { wireFrames } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client/activity";
onRecord: (result) => {
  for (const frame of wireFrames(result)) socket.send(JSON.stringify(frame));
}

// browser
import { foldFrame, type AggregatedRecord } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client/activity";
let records = new Map<string, AggregatedRecord>();
socket.onmessage = (e) => { records = foldFrame(records, JSON.parse(e.data)); };
```

Send `wireFrames(result)`, not `delta ?? current`, and don't reach past it into `result`:

- When a thinking block ends because a tool call started, that close rides in `emitted`
  while `current` is the tool — a client sending only the latter never learns the block
  finished and renders a bubble that never stops.
- `foldFrame` drops a delta whose base it has never seen (guessing at one is how you get
  text stitched onto the wrong block). `wireFrames` sends the base first, so that never
  happens on a subscriber who has been listening from the start.
- It never sends a record and a delta for the same `recordId` in one call. `foldFrame` has
  no seq guard, so a consumer would append the same text twice.

The `/activity` subpath has **no runtime imports**, so it is safe to pull into a browser
bundle. Type-only imports work anywhere today; importing the *functions* needs a bundler
that accepts `.ts` sources (Vite does; Next needs `transpilePackages`) since this package
ships source rather than a build.

A client that connects **mid-turn** needs the turn so far, or a thinking delta arrives with
nothing to append to. Subscribe first, then replay, then filter by `seq`:

```ts
const snap = session.activitySnapshot();     // { active, seq, records }
records = foldRecords(snap.records);
// then drop any streamed frame with frame.seq <= snap.seq — already reflected above
```

`seq` never restarts, so that threshold stays valid across turns. Before the first turn and
between turns `activitySnapshot()` reports `active: false` with no records: a settled turn
belongs to the transcript, not to a replay. `active` only knows what the aggregator has
been told — a hub that separately tracks which sessions are busy should trust itself.

### Debugging: the raw protocol

When an agent does something inexplicable, `wire` gives you every line in both directions,
verbatim — including the `session/update` notifications the transport takes off the wire
before the SDK sees them, which no other hook can observe.

```ts
import { createWireLog } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.kimi,
  adapterId: "kimi",
  wire: createWireLog({ path: "/tmp/acp-wire.jsonl" }),   // or { console: "stderr" }
});
```

The file is ndjson, one `WireEntry` per line, truncated per run so a log is one run's:

```bash
# The conversation as a call sequence — the view that usually finds the problem
jq -r 'select(.dir!="err") | (.line|fromjson) as $m
       | [.dir, ($m.method // (if $m.error then "error" else "result" end)),
          ($m.params.update.sessionUpdate // "")] | @tsv' /tmp/acp-wire.jsonl | uniq -c
```

```
1 out  initialize
1 in   result
1 out  session/prompt
1 in   session/update            tool_call
161 in session/update            tool_call_update     ← one call, 161 resends
1 in   session/request_permission
1 out  result
1 in   fs/write_text_file
```

That `161` is real, from a Kimi run: agents resend the whole growing tool input on every
update, which is exactly what the activity fold exists to absorb.

`dir` is `out` (to the agent's stdin), `in` (from its stdout) or `err` (its stderr). `line`
is never reserialized, so what you read is exactly what crossed the pipe. Or from the CLI:

```bash
acp-client chat --wire                  # raw lines to stderr
acp-client chat --wire=/tmp/wire.jsonl  # ndjson to a file (usable during a real conversation)
```

Off unless you set it, and the library never enables it on its own: a wire log contains
everything the agent said, file contents and command output included.

### Terminals and filesystem access

The client advertises the `terminal` and `fs` client capabilities and implements them:
agents route their shell commands through `terminal/create` and read/write files through
`fs/read_text_file` and `fs/write_text_file` on us. Terminal tool calls carry only a
`terminalId` over the wire; the client resolves the live output before handing you the
event, so `content` entries of type `terminal` come with `output`, `truncated` and
`exitStatus` filled in.

Commands run as child processes of your app, with your environment. When the agent sends
`args`, they are spawned exactly as given; when it sends none, `command` is treated as a
shell line and run through `bash` (or `/bin/sh`), because that is how agents use it —
`claude-code-acp` puts its whole Bash command line, redirections and all, in `command`.
Set `ACP_TERMINAL_SHELL` to choose a different shell.

The built-in handlers operate in the library process's host namespace. For a container,
VM, SSH session, or other runtime boundary, disable them or provide runtime-aware handlers.
Handler presence is the source of truth for capability advertisement:

```ts
new AcpClient({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.codex,
  clientHandlers: {
    terminal: false,
    filesystem: {
      readTextFile: async (request) => containerFs.read(request),
      // write omitted: writeTextFile is not advertised
    },
  },
});
```

`clientCapabilities` remains as a compatibility option. New `clientHandlers` selections
take precedence and cannot advertise an operation without installing its implementation.

### Durable sessions with a catalog

`AgentSession` gives a conversation a stable id that persists across reconnects, and
records routing metadata so you can list and resume sessions later.

```ts
import {
  AgentSession,
  ADAPTERS,
  SessionManager,
  FileSessionStore,
} from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const sessions = new SessionManager(new FileSessionStore()); // ~/.acp-lib/sessions

const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.codex,
  adapterId: "codex",
  providerSession: { kind: "new" },
  sessions,                 // ← records itself to the catalog on start & each prompt
});

await session.prompt("Start working on the auth module.");

// later. List the two separately through an Agent (`Agent.open`, see the consumer guide);
// the merged `session.listSessions()` is deprecated
const { conversations } = await agent.conversations.list(); // our catalog
for (const c of conversations) console.log(c.agentConversationId, c.agentSessionId, c.title);
for (const s of await agent.conversations.listProviderSessions()) { // the harness's own sessions
  console.log(s.providerSessionId, s.title, s.adoptedBy); // adoptedBy: the conversation that owns it, if any
}

await session.stop();
```

Logical identity and provider-thread selection are independent. `agentSessionId` is the
stable consumer handle (a UUID is minted when omitted); `providerSession` explicitly
chooses a fresh ACP thread or loads an existing one:

```ts
const record = await sessions.get(agentSessionId); // metadata only; starts nothing
if (!record) throw new Error("unknown logical session");

const reopened = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: await resolveAdapter(record.adapter),
  adapterId: record.adapter,
  agentSessionId: record.agentSessionId,
  providerSession: record.internalSessionId
    ? { kind: "load", internalSessionId: record.internalSessionId } // fails closed
    : { kind: "new" },
  mode: record.mode,
  cwd: record.cwd,
  title: record.title,
  sessions,
  ...(record.transcriptPath ? { transcriptPath: record.transcriptPath } : {}),
});
```

Loading defaults to `onFailure: "error"`. Use `onFailure: "new"` only when silently
replacing a missing provider thread is the intended policy. The legacy flat
`internalSessionId` option remains as a deprecated compatibility shorthand and retains
its historical fallback-to-new behavior.

### Optional chat transcript

Pass `transcriptPath` or `transcriptDir` to `AgentSession` to append a lightweight JSONL
chat transcript that can be read later without starting the agent. `transcriptPath` is an
exact file path chosen by the caller; `transcriptDir` lets the library write
`<agentSessionId>.jsonl` inside that directory. Supplying both is a config error.
The resolved location is available as `session.transcriptPath` and is recorded in the
session catalog when one is attached.

Transcript configuration controls history storage only. Existing transcript contents,
filenames, and directories never decide whether ACP creates or loads a provider thread.
An existing file is appended to; a missing directory/file is created on first write; and
malformed lines are skipped by readers. Omit both options to disable transcript writes—
prompting, handoff, notifications, harness commands, and catalog metadata still work.

The transcript stores user messages and final assistant replies. Set
`transcriptActivity: true` to also record tool calls, thinking and plans as `t:"activity"`
lines — `readTranscript()` still returns messages only, so read those back with
`readTranscriptLines()`.

Activity lines are **settled records, not raw deltas**: the session folds the stream and
writes checkpoints, so one shell command costs ~3 lines instead of ~15. Each line is
self-contained, and `reason` (`announced` / `input` / `settled` / `flushed` / `snapshot`)
says where in its lifecycle it was. Read them back folded — the same `recordId` last-wins
rule the live stream uses, so a reload shows what was watched:

```ts
import { readActivityRecords, readTranscriptLines, toActivityRecord } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

// just the activity state
const records = await readActivityRecords(path, { limit: 200 });  // newest 200, read backwards
for (const { recordId, reason, event } of records.values()) render(recordId, event);

// or interleave activity with messages on one timeline
for (const line of await readTranscriptLines(path, { limit: 200 })) {
  if (line.t === "msg") renderMessage(line);
  else if (line.t === "activity") renderActivity(toActivityRecord(line));
}
```

With a `limit`, the file is read **backwards from the end in chunks**, so the cost is
proportional to the page you asked for rather than to the transcript's size. Page back by
passing the oldest returned `ts` as the next `before`.

`limit` counts what you actually asked for, not raw lines — `readTranscript(path, {limit: 20})`
is twenty **messages**, however many activity lines sit between them. Narrow it yourself with
`types`, which is what makes the budget meaningful for an interleaved view:

```ts
// twenty things a chat UI would draw, with meta/raw noise excluded from the count
const page = await readTranscriptLines(path, { types: ["msg", "activity"], limit: 20 });
```

The trade-off: on an activity-heavy transcript, twenty messages may span thousands of
activity lines, so the read walks back further to find them — in the worst case to the start
of the file. Cap what gets written with `transcriptActivity: { maxBytes }` if that matters.

`t:"msg"` delimits a turn (`msg(user) → activity… → msg(assistant)`), so a trailing user
message with no reply after it means that turn died in flight — and `reason:"flushed"`
records what it was doing when it did. Pass an object instead of `true` to tune it:

```ts
transcriptActivity: {
  kinds: ["tool", "thinking"],   // default also includes plan, usage, mode, unknown
  checkpointOnInput: true,       // default: an extra line once a call knows its arguments
  rawOutput: false,              // default: it duplicates `content` byte for byte
  maxBytes: 64_000,              // default off: cap each string field, mark the line
}
```

```ts
import { AgentSession, ADAPTERS, readTranscript } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.codex,
  adapterId: "codex",
  agentSessionId: "conv-123",
  transcriptDir: "/absolute/path/to/chats",
});

await session.prompt("Summarize the repo.");

const messages = await readTranscript("/absolute/path/to/chats/conv-123.jsonl");
```

### Interactive REPL

For one stable `AgentSession`, use the opinionated session REPL. Local `/...` commands
control that logical session; explicit `//...` commands go to its active internal session;
an unknown `/...` command is reported locally and is never silently sent to the harness.

```ts
import { runAgentSessionRepl } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client/repl";
import { AgentSession, ADAPTERS } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.codex,
  adapterId: "codex",
  providerSession: { kind: "new" },
});

try {
  await runAgentSessionRepl(session, { activity: true, spinner: true });
} finally {
  await session.stop();
}
```

The older low-level controller REPL remains available as `runRepl()` plus
`createControllerCommands()`. Its `/new`, `/load`, `/resume`, and `/fork` commands replace
the `AgentController`'s ACP provider session directly; they do not manage multiple stable
`AgentSession` objects. A consumer-owned managed CLI belongs above both command sets.

### CLI

A thin wrapper over the library is exposed as `acp-client`:

```bash
acp-client chat                       # new chat with the default adapter
acp-client chat <SESSION_ID>          # resume a session
acp-client chat --adapter codex       # pick an adapter
acp-client chat --adapter pi          # @automatalabs/pi-acp (the pi-acp binary)
acp-client chat --adapter private --adapter-command '["private-agent","--acp"]'
acp-client chat --adapter private --adapter-command private-acp --pty-command private-agent
acp-client chat --exec "docker exec -i my-container"   # talk to an agent in a container
acp-client chat --cwd /workspace --approve             # auto-approve tool permissions
acp-client chat --degraded            # force degraded (PTY) mode
acp-client chat -v | -d               # verbose lifecycle / debug payloads
acp-client chat --wire[=FILE]         # dump every raw protocol line (stderr, or ndjson to FILE)
```

The managed CLI is the opinionated `SessionManager` consumer. `create`, `open` (also
`load`/`resume`), and `restore` acquire one stable logical `AgentSession` and enter its
REPL; `/...` controls that logical session and `//...` explicitly targets the active
harness thread. Lifecycle and offline inspection remain available as separate commands:

```bash
acp-client create [AGENT_SESSION_ID] --adapter opencode
acp-client open AGENT_SESSION_ID
acp-client sessions [--all] [--json]
acp-client info AGENT_SESSION_ID [--include-deleted] [--json]
```

# Agent audit log — breaking changes and release notes

Pre-1.0 changes introduced by the SQLite-backed Agent audit stream
(`.res/somelogs.md/9-16+/9-18-SPEC-agent-audit-log.md`). Fold this into the release notes.

## 1. SQLite schema version 8

Schema version 8 adds the durable Agent audit state and pending outbox. Pre-release
version-7 databases are intentionally not migrated; recreate development and smoke-test
databases before opening them with this release.

The SQLite database remains the conversation-recovery source. Audit JSONL files are an
independent operational history, not a second recovery backend.

## 2. One optional audit stream per Agent

`Agent.open()` accepts `auditLog`. Its caller-selected directory contains one logical
stream across all conversations owned by that agent, split into numbered JSONL segments.
Capture policy is evaluated from the normalized observation independently of canonical
SQLite capture, so either side may retain more detail than the other.

Canonical persistence and outbox enqueue share a transaction. Delivery happens in the
background, is ordered, durable, and at least once. Entries carry stable audit sequence,
outbox, source-observation, agent, and optional conversation identifiers.

## 3. Rotation, recovery, and observability

Size and age triggers rotate the stream without changing its identity. Startup validates
the contiguous segment set, repairs only an incomplete highest tail, and reconciles the
bounded physically written but unacknowledged suffix against SQLite. Missing delivered
history and identity conflicts fail closed.

`agent.audit` exposes `status()`, `subscribe()`, `flush()`, and `retry()`. `Agent.close()`
attempts a bounded flush and preserves undelivered rows for the next open.

`AgentAuditLogReader` provides paginated `logical` and `physical` views. Logical mode
deduplicates the bounded crash-replay window; physical mode preserves it for diagnostics.

## 4. Explicit single-owner rule

One live process owns an agent SQLite database, and one live writer owns an audit
destination. A second open fails with `AgentDatabaseInUseError` or
`AuditLogDestinationInUseError`. Any number of conversations may still execute
concurrently through that owning `Agent` instance.

## 5. Accepted initial limitations

- Audit configuration cannot change while an Agent is open.
- All numbered segments are required; automatic retention is not included.
- Enabling audit later does not backfill canonical history.
- Age rotation is evaluated on delivery, not by an idle timer.
- Files are plaintext and unsigned.
- Entry-level syncing prioritizes crash recovery over maximum raw-protocol throughput.
- Custom persistence backends cannot enable Agent audit until they implement the durable
  audit outbox contract.

The older `SessionManager` transcript/audit system remains supported and is not silently
redirected to this Agent-level stream.

# Consumer fixes (from the 2026-10-13 agents-core requirements)

Released in 0.12.0. Upgrading from 0.10.x: see `MIGRATION-0.10-to-0.12.md`.

- **Messages made of parts.** Ordered text, named paste, image, audio and file inputs; copy/link
  modes, capability checks and configurable automatic thresholds. Structured media output,
  out-of-band media, independent `capture.media`, SQLite schema 16 blob storage, reusable refs,
  byte deletion, and separate shared-file metadata listing/search. Canonical protocol/debug
  capture redacts inline bytes. Legacy positional attachments remain no-keep copies, mapped
  by MIME type; legacy JSONL stores descriptive media lines. Shared directories reach ACP
  session creation/loading. Out-of-band media waits in memory until delivered (unkept bytes are
  never written), and media an agent cannot take, or whose bytes are gone, is named instead of
  failing the turn. See the consumer guide for store and out-of-band delivery contracts.


- **Grok Build preset.** `ADAPTERS.grok` launches xAI's Grok Build over ACP
  (`grok --no-auto-update agent stdio`). A Grok session that no longer exists is recognised as
  missing, so checkpoint recovery applies to it.
- **Additional directories only when advertised.** The client sends `additionalDirectories` only to an
  agent that advertises `sessionCapabilities.additionalDirectories`, as ACP requires; otherwise they
  are left out with a warning (`additional_directories_unsupported`). Grok refused session requests
  that carried them.
- **Message boundaries.** A new tool call now ends the assistant message before it, also when the
  agent sends no message ids (before, message → tool → message was one message). Tool updates
  do not split. Applies to the live `result.messages` and to stored messages.
- **Message completion is stored when it happens.** Agent-owned conversations record a message
  `completed` when the next message or a tool call begins, with that time, instead of completing
  every message of the turn at its end with one shared timestamp. Only the turn's last message
  takes the turn's outcome; messages that ended before a failure or cancel stay `completed`.
- **Item times.** `ConversationTimelineItem` has `startedAt` (first revision) and `updatedAt`
  (latest). Presentation items have `startedAt` and `updatedAt`; their `timestamp` is now a
  deprecated alias of `updatedAt`.
- **No-op settings are not recorded.** `setConfig` with the value the option already has (and,
  with a transcript, that is already the explicit restoration target) sends, records and emits
  nothing.
- **Every record carries its operation.** Records have a typed `operationId`: the library
  operation that wrote them (turn, internal inference or recap, setting change, mode change,
  handoff). Appended out-of-band messages are standalone records without an operation id. Tool calls, permissions, thinking, activity, configuration, mode changes and protocol
  lines now carry it as messages already did. A tool call still running when its turn ends is
  recorded `failed` in that turn; an update for it in a later turn is recorded under the later
  turn. Records outside an operation have none. `records.list(id, { operationId })` filters by it.
  SQLite agent schema 15 recovers it on older records from their record ids.
- **Cancellations are recorded.** A new record kind, `cancellation` (SQLite and JSONL), with
  `requested` (reason: `steer`, `interrupt`, `stalled`, `stop`, `abort`) and `resolved`
  (outcome: `acknowledged`, `forced`, `too_late`, `failed`) revisions under the cancelled
  operation's id. After a reload a turn can still be shown as stopped or redirected. Stopping a
  conversation mid-turn records reason `stop`. SQLite schema 15
  rebuilds `conversation_records` to admit the kind. Audit capture key `cancellation`
  (default `metadata`); JSONL audit logs write it too (`t: "cancellation"`).
- **Timeline items are scoped by operation.** `reconcileConversationTimeline` keys tool call,
  permission, thinking and activity items by the record's `operationId`, so two turns that reuse a
  provider id stay two items. Items whose records carried `operationId` in their metadata keep their
  ids; the others (tool calls, for example) get new ids, so a consumer that stored timeline item ids
  sees them change once.
- **Transcript writes are serialized.** A JSONL transcript and its audit log run their writes one at
  a time. Before, a cancellation record written while an internal prompt finished could claim the
  same sequence as the prompt's reply and leave the transcript refusing every later write.
- **History pages by agent messages.** `records.listRecent(id, { agentMessages: N })` returns N
  agent messages per page with the activity that led to each, cut right after an agent message,
  with every record on the page where its item began. `fold: true` returns timeline items,
  `detail: "summary"` leaves out tool calls' input and output (`records.get` returns them), and
  `limit` caps the page (`truncated`). Without these options `listRecent` is unchanged.

# Metering — breaking changes and migration

Pre-1.0 changes introduced by the `AgentSession` metering feature
(`.res/somelogs.md/9-5+/9-6-SPEC-metering.md` §21). Fold this into the release notes.

## 1. `Usage` → `TokenUsage`, with corrected field names

The old type was wrong in three ways: it used non-ACP field names, omitted the required
`totalTokens`, and documented itself as per-turn.

```diff
-export interface Usage {
+export interface TokenUsage {
+  totalTokens: number;
   inputTokens: number;
   outputTokens: number;
-  cacheReadTokens?: number;
-  cacheWriteTokens?: number;
+  cachedReadTokens?: number;
+  cachedWriteTokens?: number;
   thoughtTokens?: number;
 }
```

`Usage` remains exported as a deprecated alias, so type-only consumers keep compiling.
Anything reading `usage.cacheReadTokens` gets `undefined` and must be renamed.

## 2. `PromptResult.usage` is a cumulative observation, not a per-turn amount

**This is the change most likely to produce silently wrong numbers.** The counters are
read as cumulative across the provider session, so summing successive reports
multiplies usage rather than accumulating it.

```ts
// WRONG — was already wrong, now demonstrably so.
let total = 0;
for (const result of results) total += result.usage?.inputTokens ?? 0;
```

```ts
// RIGHT — the library computes the per-operation delta for you.
const result = await session.prompt(text);
if (result.metering?.usage.status === "metered") {
  const used = result.metering.usage.attributable;   // this operation only
  const cost = used.ratedTotal;                      // engraved at the price in force
}
```

ACP does not actually guarantee cumulative: the SDK documents `PromptResponse.usage` as
usage "for this turn" while documenting the individual `Usage` fields as totals across
the session, and offers no discriminator. The library states the interpretation it
applied in `record.provenance.counterInterpretation` rather than pretending the protocol
settled it.

**Which reading applies is per-harness evidence, not a guess.** OpenCode was measured
reporting PER-TURN counters, so it is registered as such and its delta is the report
itself. Everything else defaults to cumulative until measured.
`MeteringConfig.counterInterpretation` overrides it for a harness version you know
differs.

`usage` is also `null` — never zero-filled — when a harness reports nothing or reports
something malformed. Null means unknown, not free.

## 3. `prompt()` and `executeInternalSessionCommand()` return `AgentSessionPromptResult`

A superset of `PromptResult`, so existing field access is unaffected. It adds
`operationId` and `metering`.

`metering` is `null` only for a prompt cancelled before it was dispatched — that
operation never reached the provider and consumed nothing, so no record is minted for it.

`AcpClient.prompt()` still returns the plain `PromptResult`.

## 4. Failed operations reject with typed errors carrying their records

```diff
 try {
   await session.prompt(text);
 } catch (err) {
-  console.error(err.message);
+  if (err instanceof AgentSessionOperationError) {
+    await usageRepository.commit(err.metering, err.metering.nextState);
+  }
+  console.error(err.message);   // preserved; original error is `err.cause`
 }
```

A failed operation can still have consumed tokens. `AgentSession.prompt()` rejects with
`AgentSessionOperationError` and `handoff()` with `AgentSessionHandoffError` (carrying
`meteringRecords`). Consumers matching on exact error identity must inspect `cause`.

## 5. New events on `AgentSessionEvent`

Exhaustive `switch` statements over the event union need new cases:
`context_window_changed`, `provider_cost_changed`, `metering_recorded`,
`metering_blocked`, `metering_unblocked`, `metering_reconciled`.

`handoff_failed` gains `meteringRecords`, and `HandoffResult` gains `meteringRecords`.

## 6. Pricing is on by default; opting out is explicit

Omitting `metering` selects best-effort enforcement with the pinned models.dev catalog.
It adds no durable storage and no transcript writes. A consumer that deliberately wants
no local rating sets `pricing: false` — which is distinct from rating that *failed*
(`pricingStatus: "pricing_unavailable"`).

Refresh the pinned catalog at release time with `bun run generate:pricing`.

## 7. Pricing sources carry two different dates

A record can now answer both "when did we capture these prices" and "how old is the price
itself" — different questions that a single timestamp conflates.

```ts
pricingCapturedAt(record.usage.attributable.pricingSource)
// pinned → generatedAt   live → fetchedAt   consumer override → null

record.usage.attributable.pricingKey.modelLastUpdated
// "2026-04-21" — when that model's entry last changed upstream
```

A catalog fetched a second ago can still carry a year-old rate, which is why the upstream
entry date is engraved beside the lookup key rather than inferred from the source.

`PricingSource` gains a third variant, `models.dev_live`, carrying `artifactSha256` and
`fetchedAt`. Exhaustive switches over the union need a new case. Live prices deliberately
do NOT use `kind: "models.dev"`: that shape promises an immutable upstream commit, and a
runtime fetch has verified none.

## 8. Records carry a provider-cost reconciliation

Every record gains `costReconciliation`, comparing the rated total against the rise in the
harness's own cumulative cost across that operation.

```ts
const check = record.costReconciliation;
if (check.status === "checked" && !check.matches) {
  // check.ratio === "2.032221" means the provider charged 2x what we accounted for
}
```

This exists because **ACP-derived metering undercounts any tool-using turn**. ACP reports
one model inference per prompt; a turn with N tool calls bills roughly N+1. Measured on
OpenCode: 1 tool call → 2.03x, 3 tool calls → 3.43x, 0 tool calls → 1.00x.

Do not bill from `attributable.ratedTotal` on the ACP backend. Bill from
`costReconciliation.providerDelta` where the harness reports cost, and treat the rated
total as the cross-check.

Agreement is judged on the ratio rounding to `1`, not on string equality: provider cost
arrives as a JSON float, so cumulative subtraction yields artifacts like
`0.002577469999999998` against an exact `0.00257747`.

## 9. `billing_required` needs a certified integration

The mode is refused unless the library has a certification registered for the adapter AND
a live `InferenceSource` presenting the matching `certificationId`. Neither a registry
entry alone nor a consumer-supplied flag opens it — certification describes evidence, not
configuration.

Only OpenCode qualifies today. For it:

```ts
const metering = await createOpencodeMetering();
const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter: ADAPTERS.opencode,
  adapterId: "opencode",
  env: metering.env,                                   // loads the plugin
  metering: {
    enforcement: "billing_required",
    inferenceSource: metering.inferenceSource,
  },
});
if (!(await metering.waitForPlugin())) throw new Error("metering plugin did not load");
```

The integration installs a plugin that observes one assistant message per model inference,
recovering the calls ACP hides. Verified against OpenCode's own database export: 9
inferences across 5 operations, cost and tokens matching exactly.

An unhealthy channel or zero observed inferences reports `usage_unavailable` and blocks in
`billing_required`, rather than falling back to a backend known to undercount.

**What blocks, and what only marks a record partial.** `billing_required` blocks on
PERMANENT loss — a report the channel refused for capacity, whose usage is accounted
nowhere. It does NOT block on an outstanding sequence gap: those usually resolve moments
later, and the late report then lands in `unallocatedUsage`, visible and costed. The
promise is "never silently under-account", not "every operation is perfectly attributed",
and halting a production session on a loopback reorder costs more than it prevents. Such
an operation still reports `attribution: "partial"`, and
`meteringSnapshot.outstandingReports` exposes the count so a consumer can alert on one
that stops falling.

A report arriving after its operation closed is routed to `unallocatedUsage` rather than
charged to whichever operation drains next — which is what makes not blocking defensible.

`routing` remains `"observed"` even here: the plugin reports what the harness ran, but a
library cannot prove no model call bypassed it.

## 10. Money totals carry their own completeness

`ratedTotal` and `ratedCosts` are no longer `Money | null` / `Money[]`. They are a
`MoneyTotal`:

```ts
interface MoneyTotal {
  readonly amounts: readonly Money[];   // one per currency
  readonly unaccounted: number;         // contributions that could not be included
}
```

```diff
-const cost = record.usage.attributable.ratedTotal?.amount;
+const cost = soleAmount(record.usage.attributable.ratedTotal)?.amount;
```

`soleAmount()` returns a figure only when exactly one currency is involved and nothing was
unaccounted; otherwise null, so the ambiguous case has to be handled rather than read as
`amounts[0]`.

Why this exists: `Money[]` had nowhere to record a contribution it failed to include, so
every accumulation site wrote `if (sum.ok) total = sum.value` and a failure silently became
a no-op. That single missing concept produced six separate under-reporting bugs — the worst
of which dropped an entire currency from an operation while reporting it fully priced.
Tokens never had the problem, because `UsageCategoryTotal` forces a coverage answer;
`addToTotal` now forces the same answer for money by returning a total rather than a
Result, so there is no `.ok` to forget.

`pricingStatus: "priced"` is now derived from the total being complete rather than from a
separate flag travelling beside it.

`unaccounted` counts contributions that were **attempted and failed**. Setting
`pricing: false` is a choice, not a failure, so a deliberately unrated session reports
`{ amounts: [], unaccounted: 0 }` — the same distinction `not_applicable` versus
`unavailable` draws for token categories. `pricingStatus` still separates the two
(`not_configured` versus `pricing_unavailable`).

`UnallocatedUsageState` loses its `costedRecordCount`/`uncostedRecordCount` counters —
`ratedCosts.unaccounted` says the same thing.

## 11. How an unrepresentable cost is reported

Nothing in the metering path turns an unknown cost into zero. Each place says so
differently, and the difference matters when reconciling against an invoice:

| where | what a consumer sees |
|---|---|
| a category could not be rated | `pricingStatus: "pricing_unavailable"` plus `pricingFailureReason` naming the category |
| one category of a priced operation | `PricedTokenAmount.pricing: null` with `reportedTokens` still present |
| a multi-model operation | top-level `pricing: null`; each rate lives in its own `lineItems` entry |
| the harness reported a malformed cost | the inference record is rejected outright; nothing partial is stored |
| the harness reported no cost | `ProviderInference.cost: null` — tokens are still recorded |
| any money total | `unaccounted` > 0 marks `amounts` as a **lower bound** |
| a total spanning currencies | `amounts` has several entries; `soleAmount()` returns null |
| provider cost vs our rating | `costReconciliation.status: "unavailable"` with a reason |

Nothing turns an unknown cost into zero, and no total can be read as complete without
saying so — `unaccounted` is on the total itself, so a lower bound cannot be mistaken for
a final figure.

## 12. Metering state starts at version 3

There is no version 1 or 2 on disk — nothing shipped before the MoneyTotal change, so
there is no migration to write. Restoration validates `version` before reading any
version-specific field; an unknown version is a preflight error in a strict mode and is
ignored wholesale in best-effort, surfaced through `session.meteringSnapshot.restoration`.

## Persisting and restoring

```ts
const initialState = await usageRepository.loadState(agentSessionId);
const session = await AgentSession.create({
  adapter,
  adapterId: "codex",
  agentSessionId,
  metering: { initialState },
});

const result = await session.prompt(text);
if (result.metering) {
  // Commit both together: a record stored without its state leaves the next session
  // with a stale baseline, which is how correct code still double-counts.
  await usageRepository.commit(result.metering, result.metering.nextState);
}
```

Enforce a unique constraint on `operationId` to make delivery idempotent. See
`smoke-tests/test6-metering/` for a runnable version of this contract.

# Operation lifecycle

Released in 0.12.0 (it landed on `beta` while the package version still read 0.11.2).

Provider turns, internal inference and adoption recaps now expose their current operation stage and
last output time. Silent inference requests fail with `OperationStalledError` (`code: stalled`), carrying
the silence phase, captured messages, operation ID and metering record. Agent-owned conversations
persist an error record and mark any partial assistant reply failed.

Cancellation answers pending permissions as cancelled, aborts the handler's optional second
`AbortSignal` argument, resends the notification halfway through the adapter's grace period, and
force-stops an unresponsive process. Cancelled prompt results expose `cancel: acknowledged | forced`.
Interrupt and steer results keep their normal cancelled behavior after a forced stop.

The next provider operation reconnects automatically after an exit or forced stop. It first loads the
same session; Agent-owned conversations can recover from a checkpoint under their existing recovery
policy, preserving the conversation object. Observe `state.providerConnection` and
`provider_reconnected` (`via: loaded | recovered`). Consumers that previously retired a disconnected
conversation can now keep it and send the next prompt normally. A failed reconnect is retryable on the
next operation. When the provider no longer has the session, the conversation applies the rule it
applies at open: Agent-owned checkpoint recovery, SessionManager continuation strategies, or
`providerSession.onFailure` without transcript persistence (`"new"` reports `via: fresh`). With nothing
left, the conversation reports `continuation_unavailable` instead of failing every prompt.
SessionManager's manual recovery after the library process itself dies is unchanged.

After a turn the provider received ends in a stall or error, explicit queue messages are held (a prompt
that fails before reaching the provider holds nothing). Pending steers up to the next queued message run
after recovery as one prompt with `via: stall`; the next consumer turn that completes releases the held
queue (internal prompts such as a recap do not). Inspect `state.pendingHold`,
`pendingMessages[].heldBy`, and `message_held` / `message_released` events. With `busyDelivery: queue`,
every prompt sent after a failure joins the hold, so the conversation stays held until you send one prompt
with `delivery: steer` (or withdraw). Withdrawal still works.

Configure `AgentConfig.operationLifecycle` (or the same field on a detached conversation) with
`turns`, `internalInference`, and `recap`. First/next-output limits default to 120/180 seconds;
`false` disables an individual inference limit. Tools and permissions explain silence and suspend
those limits; optional `toolMs` bounds a tool. Adapter `cancelGraceMs` defaults to 30 seconds.
Control requests (initialize, new, load, list, delete, config, authenticate) have no deadline: they end when the
harness answers or the process exits.

Codex measurements on 2026-10-18 (three throwaway sessions, default model): first protocol output
8–12ms, longest observed tool-free silence 3260–4128ms, acknowledged cancel 32–72ms, and session load
514–621ms. Claude (three sessions): first output 3–15ms, silence 1989–4296ms, cancel 4–5ms, and load 828–848ms. These are short-history measurements and do not cover automatic compaction; conservative
defaults are retained. See `smoke-tests/test13-operationLifecycle/` for reproducible scenarios and results.

Known measurement gaps: OpenCode's default upstream refused ACP model calls under its free-tier
policy. Codex's permission smoke prompt did not generate a native permission request; the mock
permission scenario verifies cancellation and handler aborts. Initialization excludes launcher
preparation; downloads inside a spawned installer command still count unless moved into launcher
preparation. Turn-ending persistence beyond the existing message status remains the separate
requirement 3 referenced by the lifecycle spec.

Degraded PTY mode observes raw terminal output for visibility and keeps output silence deadlines
disabled by default because it has no ACP tool/permission signals. Explicit limits still apply there,
and cancellation remains bounded. Handoff operations use the target adapter's cancellation grace.

A separate Codex run with 24 additional short turns replayed 53 updates in 554ms (maximum replay gap
535ms, including initial wait). No automatic-compaction stress run was performed.

`AgentConversation.listSessions()` is deprecated. It merges the library's catalog with the harness's
session list into one `MergedSession` shape, and when the harness listing fails it returns the catalog
half without saying so. Use `agent.conversations` for conversations and
`agent.conversations.listProviderSessions()` for harness sessions; that one reports listing failures.
A failed harness listing in `listSessions()` now throws instead of returning the catalog half silently.

# Consumer guide

This guide is for applications embedding `@qlairoslabs/acp-client`, especially
orchestrators that own several agents and conversations. The recommended durable API is
`Agent`, backed by a caller-located SQLite database. The library owns ACP communication,
conversation queues, typed records, search, identity lifecycle hooks, and persistence.
The consumer owns database placement, adapter definitions, user interface, and application
policy.

`AgentSession` remains the compatibility name for one live `AgentConversation`. The
older `SessionManager`/JSONL workflow is still supported and documented later in this
guide, but new durable applications should normally begin with `Agent`.

The package requires Bun 1.3.5 or newer.

## Mental model

There are three primary runtime layers:

| Layer | Main API | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Agent identity and persistence | `Agent` | Own SQLite persistence, adapter registry, identity runtime, and conversations |
| One stable conversation | `AgentConversation` (`AgentSession` compatibility alias) | Prompt, interrupt, handoff, switch adapters, reset, observe state, and configure the harness |
| Active harness thread | ACP and `internalSessionCommands` | Harness-specific commands such as `/usage` and `/model` |

An `agentSessionId` (`ags-*`) identifies the agent. An `agentConversationId` (`agc-*`)
identifies one of its conversations. An `internalSessionId` identifies the replaceable
provider or harness thread behind that conversation.

```text
consumer
  └── Agent ags-…                           stable agent identity + SQLite database
        └── AgentConversation agc-…         stable conversation identity
              └── AgentController
                    └── internal thread abc replaceable harness identity
```

## Install and import

```bash
bun add @qlairoslabs/acp-client
```

```ts
import {
  ADAPTERS,
  Agent,
  AgentAuditLogReader,
  AgentSession,
  AuditLogReader,
  SessionManager,
  TranscriptReader,
  formatResponseMessages,
  type Adapter,
  type AgentSessionOpenStage,
  type AgentSessionNotification,
  type PromptHandlers,
} from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";
```

## Start with one SQLite-backed agent

The database path is explicit and belongs to the consumer. One database contains one
agent identity and any number of independently addressable conversations.

```ts
import { Agent, ADAPTERS } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const agent = await Agent.open({
  persistence: {
    kind: "sqlite",
    path: "/absolute/path/to/state/atlas.sqlite",
  },
  adapters: {
    codex: ADAPTERS.codex,
  },
  defaultAdapterId: "codex",
});

try {
  const conversation = await agent.conversations.create();
  const result = await conversation.prompt("hi");

  for (const message of result.messages) {
    console.log(message.text);
  }
} finally {
  await agent.close();
}
```

The user message and each assistant-message boundary are stored as separate typed rows.
Reopen the same database with `Agent.open()` and call
`agent.conversations.open(agentConversationId)` to continue its active provider thread.
`Agent.close()` interrupts live prompts and waits for their finalization and queued
conversation writes before closing the SQLite backend; an interrupted prompt may reject.

A newly created conversation may expose `conversation.internalSessionId` immediately, but
the provider attachment is retained only in memory until its first completed provider turn.
If the conversation stops before then, reopening the durable `agc-*` conversation creates a
fresh provider thread. After a completed turn, the provider mapping becomes the continuation
candidate used by `open()`; successfully loading it does not create another history row.
This is a local evidence threshold, not a guarantee that the harness will keep the provider
session loadable forever.

### Attach consumer data to a prompt message

The object-form prompt APIs attach opaque JSON to the submitted **user message**:

```ts
await conversation.prompt({
  text: "hello",
  consumerMetadata: { deliveryId: "delivery-42", submittedBy: "relay" },
});
await conversation.promptFrom({
  participantId: "agent-bob",
  text: "Can you review this?",
  consumerMetadata: { deliveryId: "delivery-43" },
});

const messages = await agent.persistence.messages.list(conversation.id);
console.log(messages.messages[0]?.consumerMetadata);
```

The older positional `prompt(text, handlers?, attachments?)` and
`promptFrom(participantId, text, handlers?, attachments?)` calls remain valid.
`consumerMetadata` is stored in `conversation_messages.consumer_metadata_json` and
returned as `MessageRecord.consumerMetadata`; it is not copied onto assistant messages,
sent to the provider, added to identity context, or indexed for search. The library does
not interpret its fields. The separate envelope `metadata` field still carries older
library-owned operation correlation. A raw audit capture includes consumer metadata;
content/metadata audit capture omits it.

### Messages made of parts

`prompt({ parts })` accepts ordered `MessagePart` values. An optional `text` is a leading text
part; `pasted` retains its optional name and is sent as text. The text-only `result.text` view
and positional calls remain available. A response containing media also has ordered
`result.messages[i].parts`; streaming `onResponseChunk` exposes each non-text `part`.

```ts
await conversation.prompt({
  parts: [
    { kind: "text", text: "Review this plot and these notes." },
    { kind: "image", path: "plot.png" },
    { kind: "pasted", name: "notes", text: "The red line is the baseline." },
    { kind: "file", path: "/shared/report.pdf", mode: "link" },
  ],
});
```

Media kinds are `image`, `audio`, and `file`. Each input has exactly one source: `data:
Uint8Array`, `path` (relative to the conversation's working directory, absolute, or a `file://`
URI), or `ref` (a previously kept copy). MIME types are inferred from file paths; supply the
MIME type for byte-array inputs when known. SVG is a `file` and is embedded as markup, retaining
its MIME type. Text files are ACP embedded text resources; other files use blob resources.
An embedded copy's uri is `attachment:///<name>`: it names the copy, not a file the agent could
open. A UI rendering SVG must sanitize it.

Some adapters drop kinds they advertise. Claude's (`claude-agent-acp`, checked at 0.85.0) keeps
embedded text files but silently drops binary ones (PDFs, any blob), although it advertises
`embeddedContext`, so the model never sees them and nothing fails. Send binary files to Claude as
links (`mode: "link"`, a file it can reach): its Read tool opens PDFs. Whether a model reads a
kind also depends on the model: OpenCode on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has no PDF input.

`mode: "copy"` sends the actual content. `keep: false` records name, MIME type, size and SHA-256
without retaining bytes; the default keeps bytes when a store is available. `mode: "link"`
requires a path and sends an absolute `file://` resource link. It records a pointer, so later
edits/deletion of the original affect what history can display. The library does not open a
link: one whose file cannot be read is still sent, with no size. `keep` is invalid on links.
A link the agent sends without a size is recorded without one.
`record: false` sends a part without recording it and cannot be combined with `keep`.

With no mode, path sources use copies up to 100,000 bytes for files, 3,750,000 for images and
5,000,000 for audio; larger paths use links. Configure these byte thresholds on the Agent with
`media: { thresholds: { file, image, audio } }`. Byte-array and ref sources remain copies.
There is no library size ceiling. Provider errors surface to the caller. Unsupported explicit
copies are refused using the agent's prompt capabilities; an automatic path source falls back
to a link. PTY mode refuses media parts.

Declare shared directories with `conversationDefaults: { additionalDirectories: ["/shared"] }`
or a conversation's `runtime.additionalDirectories`. They are sent only to an agent that advertises
`sessionCapabilities.additionalDirectories` (otherwise left out, with a warning). They reach ACP session creation/load;
the harness applies its own permissions. The library does not restrict pointers. A harness on
another machine or in an isolated container needs a shared mount or a copy.

SQLite schema 16 stores kept blobs separately from message rows in the same database and
transaction. History and audit records contain refs/URIs and metadata. Ordinary text messages
remain strings; mixed messages use `PersistedContentBlock[]`, including `media` and `pasted`.
Old inline image/resource blocks can still be read; migration rebuilds structured message
search text and its FTS index without old inline bytes or refs. Raw canonical protocol capture and debug
prompt logs redact inline media; a consumer's explicitly requested `wire` callback is verbatim.

```ts
const agent = await Agent.open({
  // ...persistence, adapters, and other settings...
  capture: { message: "content", media: "metadata" },
  // media: { store: yourMediaStore }, // optional MediaStore override
});

const store = agent.media.store ?? agent.persistence.media;
const saved = await store?.get(ref); // { ref, info, data } or null when removed
await conversation.prompt({ parts: [{ kind: "image", ref }] });
await agent.deleteMedia(ref); // removes bytes; history retains the dangling ref
await agent.deleteMediaForConversation(conversation.id);

const files = await agent.persistence.files?.search({
  text: "plot", agentConversationId: conversation.id, kind: "image", minSize: 1,
});
```

`capture.media` is `none`, `metadata`, or `content` (default), independently of message text.
The conversation persistence resolver can override it, and a part's own `record`/`keep` wins.
Checkpointing still summarizes text. A backend without `media` and no override defaults to
metadata; explicit `keep: true` is refused. The older SessionManager/AgentSession JSONL
transcript records text and descriptive part lines, with no media store.

A `MediaStore` implements async `put(bytes, info) -> ref`, `get(ref)`, `delete(ref)` and
`list(owner)`. `get` returns `{ ref, info, data }` or null; `list` returns `{ ref, info }`
entries. Preserve all `MediaInfo` fields. Separate stores cannot share the record transaction: failed
writes stop dispatch, and `list(owner)` supports orphan cleanup. Reusing a kept ref within
its conversation reuses bytes; another conversation gets a new copy. Copies record SHA-256
but are not deduplicated. Clearing records deletes SQLite media; the Agent clear API also
cleans an overridden store. Soft deletion retains media.

`files.list` and `files.search` browse media metadata, including unkept/deleted copies and
links, with optional conversation, name, kind, MIME type and size filters. They accept `limit`
and `cursor`; response revisions are folded. Message search covers text and pasted text,
without indexing media names, refs or bytes. Offset file cursors can shift under concurrent
inserts. Custom backends can supply the optional `files` repository.

SQLite keeps ordering and type-specific content separate. `conversation_records` is a
narrow canonical envelope containing the conversation-local sequence, kind, timestamp,
operation correlation, and optional metadata. Every envelope has exactly one typed detail
row in tables such as `conversation_messages`, `conversation_tool_call_events`, or
`conversation_activity_events`. A mixed timeline is read as one envelope page followed by
bounded, batched subtype hydration; it never performs one query per record.

Messages store ordinary text directly in `content_text`; structured or multimodal content
uses `content_json`. Tool calls, permissions, configuration, actions, thinking, and
activities retain meaningful lifecycle transitions as independently sequenced records.
Raw ACP protocol bodies remain JSON because their external shape is intentionally open.
Each completed metered operation adds an ordered `metering` reference whose complete
financial record remains in `metering_records`; the timeline does not duplicate billing
payloads.

`activity` is reserved for model activity such as plans. Complete session observations
such as usage, available commands, mode/config announcements, session metadata, echoed
user messages, and unknown protocol updates are not reclassified as model activity.
Their semantic state is retained by the relevant configuration, metering, or checkpoint
storage, while consumers that need exact diagnostic traffic can enable protocol capture.

SQLite protocol capture supports `"none"`, `"metadata"`, and `"raw"`; protocol
`"content"` is rejected because coalesced content already belongs to the typed semantic
records. Exact method filters provide a compact protocol skeleton without persisting the
high-volume update stream:

```ts
capture: {
  protocol: {
    level: "metadata",
    excludeMethods: ["session/update"],
  },
}
```

`includeMethods` is also available and cannot be combined with `excludeMethods`. Both use
exact ACP method names. Methodless JSON-RPC responses remain captured because their method
cannot be determined without correlating request IDs. Filtering happens before canonical
sequence allocation, so omitted frames create neither rows nor sequence gaps.

FTS5 indexes deliberately extracted searchable text rather than serialized record JSON.
The initial indexes cover messages, tool calls, and activities. Consumer metadata and raw
protocol bodies are not searched implicitly.

Schema version 11 adds stable assistant-message identities and migrates version-8,
version-9, and version-10 agent databases in place. Version 10 added message consumer
metadata. Pre-release version-7 SQLite files are not migrated because
they were used only by development smoke tests; opening one gives a recreate instruction.

### Read SQLite conversation history and previews

`records.listRecent()` returns the newest matching records at a fixed conversation
sequence snapshot. Each page is oldest-first for rendering; its `olderCursor` stays
bound to that snapshot and kind filter even if new records arrive:

```ts
import { reconcileConversationTimeline } from "@qlairoslabs/acp-client";

const first = await agent.persistence.records.listRecent!(conversation.id, { limit: 50 });
let items = reconcileConversationTimeline([], first.records);
const older = first.olderCursor
  ? await agent.persistence.records.listRecent!(conversation.id, {
      limit: 50,
      olderCursor: first.olderCursor,
    })
  : null;
if (older) items = reconcileConversationTimeline(items, older.records);
```

Paging by records cuts turns anywhere: a tool call is several records, so a page can start
mid-turn. To page by what the conversation shows, count agent messages instead:

```ts
const page = await agent.persistence.records.listRecent!(conversation.id, {
  agentMessages: 50,  // each page: 50 agent messages and the activity that led to each
  fold: true,         // timeline items instead of records
  detail: "summary",  // tool calls without input and output
});
let items = page.items;
// Expanding a step: its full record merges into the summary item.
const full = await agent.persistence.records.get(step.current.recordId);
items = reconcileConversationTimeline(items, [full!]);
```

- The cut goes right after an agent message (out-of-band appends count), so a page usually
  begins with a turn's user message, and activity after the newest message (a running turn)
  stays on the newest page.
- A record goes to the page where its item's first revision falls. A page holds every revision
  of its items, including later ones up to the snapshot, and none of another page's: a message
  that completed after the next tool started is not split across pages.
- `limit` caps the page (records, or items when folded; default 2000). A page that reaches it
  ends at a whole item with `truncated: true`, and `olderCursor` continues from there.
- `fold: true` returns `ConversationTimelineItem`s; live records still merge with
  `reconcileConversationTimeline(items, records)`. With `detail: "summary"` an item keeps two
  revisions, its first (its start) and its merged current (under its latest revision's id),
  so it reconciles like any other item.
- `detail: "summar
…[文件过长——仅保留首 16KB 与末 8KB]…

transaction. A failure after the transcript header is installed can leave an initialized
artifact which must be opened or cleaned up explicitly. Direct audit persistence is
rejected instead of creating an audit file which the live session cannot safely own.

For durable persistent applications, use `SessionManager.createAgentSession()` and
`SessionManager.loadAgentSession()`. The manager owns prepared creation, registry fencing,
audit attachment, retry discovery, and completion receipts.

## Legacy compatibility

`FileSessionStore`, `sessions:`, `transcriptPath`, `transcriptDir`, and
`transcriptActivity` remain for compatibility with the earlier flat catalog/transcript
model. They should not be used for new managed implementations.

Legacy transcript conversion and registry import are explicit:

```ts
await migrateLegacyTranscript(options);
await sessions.importLegacySessions(legacyStore);
```

Migration preserves the legacy prefix for presentation and establishes a new V2 authority
boundary. Strict V2 creation never claims an already initialized legacy file implicitly.

## Current V0 boundaries

- Managed creation and loading support normal ACP mode only.
- Direct V2 creation supports transcript-only persistence and is not crash-resumable;
  direct V2 audit persistence is rejected.
- Direct V2 opening currently requires an explicit `agentSessionId` and transcript;
  checkpoint-only and exact-file identity inference are deferred.
- Handoff creates a new thread on the current adapter.
- Tombstone restoration currently loads only the recorded provider thread; reconstruction
  strategies remain available to ordinary managed loading but are deferred for restoration.
- Transcript and audit reconfiguration are separate operations.
- Replacement reconfiguration retains the existing artifact path.
- Generic ACP load cannot prove what happened after a crash; uncertainty requires an
  explicit consumer decision.
- Session logs are plaintext and do not provide encryption or tamper resistance.
- Metering records are application telemetry, not an invoice or trusted billing ledger.
- A transcript or audit generation has one active writer, enforced by a writer lock.
- Retention policy and automatic pruning belong to the consumer.

## Recommended ownership rules

- Key application state by `agentSessionId`, never `internalSessionId`.
- Keep live `AgentSession` objects in the consumer; use the manager for durable discovery.
- Resolve adapter IDs in the consumer and fail explicitly when one is unknown.
- Inspect `AgentSessionOpenResult.promptability` before dispatching work.
- Read state before subscribing so no initial snapshot is missed.
- Persist operation metering records separately when they matter financially.
- Use transcript presets deliberately; detailed and diagnostic capture can contain secrets.
- Keep local commands distinct from harness commands.
- Stop every live session during application shutdown.
- Do not infer provider loading from a transcript path or file contents.

## Operation lifecycle and automatic provider recovery

`conversation.state.operation` is null when no model request is running. While running it exposes
`operationId`, `kind`, `stage`, `startedAt`, `lastOutputAt`, `toolsInFlight` and optional cancellation
reason/time. `operation_stage_changed` fires on stage changes; read the snapshot for current output
timestamps. Internal-inference attempt handles expose the same information at `handle.snapshot.operation`.

Set `operationLifecycle` on `Agent.open()` or a detached conversation:

```ts
operationLifecycle: {
  turns: { firstOutputMs: 120_000, nextOutputMs: 180_000 },
  internalInference: { firstOutputMs: 120_000 },
  recap: { nextOutputMs: 180_000 },
}
```

Individual inference limits accept `false`; tools and pending permissions suspend output deadlines.
`toolMs` is optional and disabled by default. Each adapter may set `cancelGraceMs` (default 30 seconds).
Permission handlers may accept a second optional AbortSignal; discard UI and stop asynchronous work
when it aborts. A late permission answer cannot change the cancelled outcome.

A stalled turn rejects with `OperationStalledError`, including `phase` (`no_response` or
`incomplete_response`), `messages`, `operationId`, `metering` and optional `followedBy` steer IDs.
Its partial response is failed, and its metering outcome is cancelled. Forced interrupts and steers
resolve cancelled and expose `cancel: forced`; acknowledged cancellation reports `acknowledged`.

After a provider exit or forced stop, keep the conversation and send the next prompt. The library
loads its provider session automatically and emits `provider_reconnected` with `via: loaded` or
`recovered` (Agent-owned checkpoint recovery under the configured policy). The snapshot connection
moves through `disconnected`, `reconnecting`, and `connected`. A transient reconnect failure fails
that prompt, and the next prompt tries again.

When the harness no longer has the session, the conversation applies the same rule it applies when
opened: checkpoint recovery for Agent-owned conversations (`onLoadFailure: "recover"`), the
`continuation.strategies` list for SessionManager conversations (only `new_from_transcript` or a
consumer continuation can replace the session; the default list is load only), and
`providerSession.onFailure` otherwise (`"new"` starts a fresh session without the earlier context and
reports `via: fresh`). When the rule has nothing left, the prompt rejects with the reason, `promptability`
reports `continuation_unavailable`, and later prompts are refused until the conversation is reopened
with a different policy. SessionManager's existing library-crash uncertainty recovery remains separate.

Harness behaviours seen after a crash (test13, 2026-10-19):

- **OpenCode finishes the interrupted turn first.** When a reloaded session has a turn that was cut
  off (the process was killed or frozen mid-turn), OpenCode completes that interrupted request before
  answering the next prompt. The reply to the next prompt can therefore start with the old turn's
  output, and it can be silent for longer than usual while the old request runs. The failed turn was
  already reported as an error; treat the start of the next reply accordingly, and keep the silence
  limits generous on OpenCode (the defaults are).
- **Codex archives a deleted session.** Loading it fails until it is unarchived with
  `codex unarchive <id>`; the library treats it as missing, so the conversation's continuation rule
  applies (a replacement session, when the rule provides one).

After a turn the provider received fails (stalled, crashed, or errored), queued messages remain held.
A prompt that fails before reaching the provider holds nothing. Read `state.pendingHold`,
`pendingMessages[].heldBy` and the `message_held` / `message_released` events. Steers waiting after a
stall are sent as the recovery prompt, up to the next queued message (not including it); steers after
that message run after it. Send a message with `delivery: steer` to continue; its successful
completion releases queued messages in order (internal prompts such as a recap do not release). Explicit queue delivery while held
adds to the hold, including when idle. `withdraw()` remains available.

**If your default is `busyDelivery: "queue"`**, every prompt sent after a failure joins the hold, so
nothing runs until you send a prompt with `delivery: "steer"` explicitly (or withdraw). Give the user
a way to send that steer, for example when `state.pendingHold` is set. These message events are live
observations; consumers may store them if needed.

Control requests (initialize, new, load, list, delete, config, authenticate) have no deadline. They
end when the harness answers or when the process exits. A large session can take a minute or more to
load; that is not treated as a failure.

Degraded PTY mode observes raw terminal output but cannot identify ACP tools or permissions. Its
output silence limits are disabled by default to preserve long-running tools; explicit configured
limits still apply, and cancellation is bounded.

# Migrating from 0.10.2 to 0.12.0

For agents-core and the webapp, which pin `@qlairoslabs/acp-client` `0.10.2`. This covers everything
since: `0.11.0`, the operation lifecycle (`0.11.2`), and the work done for the 2026-10-13
requirements list. `CONSUMER_GUIDE.md` is the full reference; this file says what changed and what to do
about it.

**Status.** 0.12.0 is on the library's `beta` branch, not yet pushed or published. Until it is,
point agents-core at a local checkout of the library to try it.

## Before you upgrade

- **Back up the SQLite agent databases.** Opening one migrates it to schema 16 (from 14, through 15).
  The migration is one way: an older library refuses the migrated file.
  - Schema 15 rebuilds `conversation_records` to admit a new record kind, and recovers `operationId` on
    older records from their record ids.
  - Schema 16 adds a blob table for kept media and an out-of-band delivery table, and rebuilds the
    message full-text index without inline bytes. On a large database the first open takes longer.
- JSONL transcripts and audit logs need no migration; they gain new line types (below).
